title: Spacing and Interleaving Effects Require Distinct Theoretical Bases: A Systematic Review Testing the Cognitive Load and Discriminative-Contrast Hypotheses
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 21, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarises a systematic review by Chen, Pass and Sweller arguing that spacing and interleaving, though often lumped together, work through different cognitive mechanisms and need to be understood separately. Spaced practice, they argue, works because rest periods let depleted working memory resources recover; interleaved practice works through a discriminative-contrast effect, which helps learners tell similar concepts apart. Crucially, spacing needs an actual rest-from-deliberate-learning period, such as sleep, breaks, or unrelated activity, to work, while interleaving is most effective specifically when the mixed topics are similar enough that discrimination between them is genuinely useful — dissimilar topics don't benefit as much. Barton draws the practical distinction for teachers: use spacing when students need a cognitive breather, and use interleaving specifically when students are prone to confusing closely related concepts.
points: Spacing and interleaving are driven by different mechanisms — working memory recovery for spacing, discriminative contrast for interleaving — and shouldn't be treated as interchangeable.
Spacing's rest periods must be free of deliberate learning to have the working-memory-recovery effect; filling rest periods with more study defeats the purpose.
Interleaving works best specifically when the mixed topics are similar and easily confused; very dissimilar topics see less benefit from interleaving.
The spacing effect has been observed with rest periods as short as 30 seconds or as long as several days, giving teachers real flexibility in how they implement it.
quotes: The researchers suggest that spaced practice, where learning sessions are separated by periods of rest, works by allowing depleted working memory resources to recover, while interleaved practice, where different topics are mixed together during learning, relies on a discriminative-contrast effect, which helps learners differentiate between similar concepts.
Spaced practice, which involves alternating periods of learning with periods of rest, can enhance student learning.
When implementing spaced practice, the rest periods should not be filled with other learning activities.
Interleaving is most effective when the interleaved topics are similar and require students to learn to discriminate between them.
Teachers should consider the cognitive demands of the tasks they are teaching when deciding whether to use spaced or interleaved practice.
The data of this review suggest that the spacing effect needs a rest-from-deliberate-learning period between learning episodes
